title: What Actually Multiplies When We Call Someone 10x
summary: Where the 10x number came from, what a study of 1,000+ open-source projects found about heroes, and the habits that really multiply a team's work.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Thirty minutes into an incident, a teammate stops typing and starts drawing the request path in a notebook. They ask two questions, spot a stale cache key, suggest a rollback and write a three-line note so the next on-call person recognizes the pattern sooner. By dinner, someone in the team chat calls them a 10x developer.

They earned the compliment. Still, nobody was ten times faster than anyone else in that half hour. They knew the system, asked the right questions and left something behind for the team. That's worth unpacking, because the 10x label hides exactly the parts you can learn.

Where the number comes from

The idea goes back to a 1968 study by Sackman, Erickson and Grant. The fun part is that they weren't studying individual differences at all. They wanted to know whether programming online beat programming offline, and the gaps between individual programmers drowned out the effect they were looking for. Steve McConnell, who spread the 10x figure through Code Complete, sums up the best-to-worst ratios they found: about 20:1 in initial coding time, 25:1 in debugging time and 5:1 in program size. He also admits the study had flaws, such as lumping together people using low-level and high-level languages (Origins of 10X: How Valid is the Underlying Research?).

Two details get lost every time the number travels. First, it compares the best and the worst people in a group, not the best and the average. In DeMarco and Lister's study of 166 professional programmers, which McConnell also cites, the gap among people who finished the task was 5.6x, and about 10% didn't finish at all. Second, the research itself is disputed. Laurent Bossavit went through McConnell's citations in a 2010 critique (later part of The Leprechauns of Software Engineering) and argued that they don't support the claim. McConnell answered point by point and puts the range across his sources at roughly 5:1 to 25:1.

So people really do differ a lot. "This person does the work of ten average engineers" is a much bigger claim than any of that data makes.

Speed is mostly context

A senior who knows the product history, the deploy pipeline, the usual failure modes, the database's weird corners and what customers complain about can move very fast. From the outside it looks like raw talent. A lot of it is memory: years of incidents, reviews and hallway questions packed into judgment. It's also why the "10x" person on one team can feel pretty ordinary for their first few months at a new company.

Big impact rarely means writing ten times more code, either. Often the high-impact move is deleting a bad abstraction, saying no to a migration that adds more risk than value, or teaching three teammates to debug a service on their own. Someone who makes five people a little better can add more than whoever closed the most tickets.

What the hero research found

Here's a twist. Lots of GitHub projects are "hero projects," where about 20% of developers make 80% or more of the contributions. Earlier research mostly treated that as a risk, since everything funnels through a few people. Suvodeep Majumder, Tim Menzies and colleagues analyzed over 1,000 open-source projects and compared two measures: how much a developer changes other people's code ("hero-ness") and how much they comment on other people's issues ("social-ness"). Social-ness was the statistically stronger predictor of code quality, measured as bug counts. The authors' advice: to build better code, build better communication flows between the core developers and everyone else (Communication and Code Dependency Effects on Software Code Quality).

That matches what most of us see at work. The heroes who help a project are the ones information flows through. Trouble starts when it stops at them.

When the label starts to hurt

If the team believes one person is the only one who can save the system, people stop investing in docs, onboarding, tests and pairing. Why bother, they'll handle it. The hero becomes a bottleneck, then a risk, then a tired person who can't take a proper vacation. A team that leans on one brilliant engineer is fragile, however good the story sounds.

The label also rewards visible rescue over invisible prevention. Whoever fixes the midnight incident gets the applause. Whoever designed the safer rollout that prevented five incidents gets nothing, because nothing broke. Teams that only celebrate firefighting tend to get more fires. (If your top performer is also hard to work with, that's a separate problem, covered in When Your Best Engineer Is Hard to Work With.)

The myth discourages everyone else, too. If excellence is a mysterious gift, the road to it looks closed. Yet most of the habits behind high impact can be learned: read the code before rewriting it, ask what failure would look like, write decisions down, keep PRs small, fix the doc the second time a question comes up, automate the chore everyone hates, learn the business rules behind the code. None of it is dramatic. All of it compounds.

Look for multipliers

Exceptional engineers exist. Some people have deep taste and patience, and can connect product, architecture and people in a way that changes where a project goes. The useful question is what lets that impact spread instead of piling up in one person. Does the team give them time to teach? Does it copy their patterns into docs and tooling? Does it keep them from becoming the permanent emergency exit? I wrote about this through Sun Wukong, a classic 10x talent who still needed a headband, in Sun Wukong at Work.

And if you want more high-impact work from your team, look at friction first. Often the fastest route is removing whatever drags people down to 0.5x: unclear ownership, slow builds, noisy alerts, vague requirements.

Try this week

  • Next time someone gets called 10x, name what actually multiplied: context, judgment, teaching or prevention.
  • Write down one thing about your system that only you know, and put it where others will find it.
  • Pair with a teammate on the next bug you'd normally fix alone.
  • Thank someone in public for an incident that didn't happen.
  • Pick one 0.5x drag (a slow build, a noisy alert) and open a ticket to fix it.

faqs.a: Large differences between programmers are well documented, but the famous ratios compare the best and the worst people in a group, not the best and the average. Steve McConnell puts the range across the studies he cites at about 5:1 to 25:1, and critics such as Laurent Bossavit argue much of that research is weak. Read 10x as "people differ a lot," not as a measured constant.

faqs.q: Where does the 10x claim come from?
faqs.a: From a 1968 study by Sackman, Erickson and Grant. They set out to compare online and offline programming and found that differences between individual programmers were far larger than the effect they meant to measure. Steve McConnell later spread the figure through Code Complete.

faqs.q: Are hero developers bad for a project?
faqs.a: Not by themselves. A study of over 1,000 open-source projects found that how much developers communicate on issues predicted code quality (bug counts) better than how much a few heroes change other people's code. The risk comes when knowledge stops with one person instead of flowing through them.
